about: Every vector of this folder. A vector is checked against a rule that no schema can state (conformance/rules.py), named by 'rule'. call.profile: one tool call as an engine wrote it (tool, cwd, input_text) and the text that is bound for it (call_text: its cwd, input and tool, as one object, as RFC 8785 writes it), or the code it is refused with. approval.binding: one approval record of the right shape, and exactly what does not agree inside it (an empty list when everything does); effect_text, where present, is the text whose UTF-8 bytes the digest is taken over. approval.lifecycle: one request, then calls on it one after another, each with who is calling, the answer, and the record after it. The call texts, the effect texts, three whole sets of lines and the order of the answers were written by hand and then checked against the rule, not copied from it. queue.delivery: one queued message and what happens to it, step by step: the item after each step, or the code the step is refused with; a step may carry the event of the log that belongs to it, and an acceptance always carries its input.accepted event. task.derivation: a run's view or a session and one of its turns, the log, the approvals pending, a Task, and exactly which of the Task's fields are not what the source says (an empty list when all are). These files are plain ASCII: a character outside it is written as a JSON escape.

vectors.shows: A plain call: keys come out sorted, with no spaces, whatever order and spacing the engine used.

Numbers are written as ECMAScript writes them: 1.0 is 1, 1e-7 stays 1e-7, 1E3 is 1000, minus zero is 0, 1e21 is 1e+21. Two serialisers that spell a number differently (1.0 against 1, 1e-07 against 1e-7) cannot give two digests, because neither spelling is what is hashed.
Keys are ordered by their UTF-16 code units, not by code point: U+10000 sorts before U+E000. (A sort by code point would put them the other way round.)
A string has one spelling: the engine wrote the letter a as an escape, and the bound text holds the letter.
The same call as p04, written plainly by the engine: the same text, so the same digest.

Accented text in the tool's name, in the directory (a Windows path, with backslashes) and in the input, and a character above U+FFFF: each stands as itself. No field of an engine's call is held to one alphabet.
A tab keeps its short escape; any other character below U+0020 is a lower-case \u escape; U+007F stands as itself in the bound text (the lines a surface prints escape it: see the approval vectors).
Arrays keep their order; objects inside are sorted too; true, false and null are themselves.
The letter e with an acute accent written as one character, and written as e followed by a combining accent, are two different strings and stay two: the core never normalises.
An object that names a key twice is refused: the core never picks the first or the last.
The same, at any depth.
NaN is not JSON.
Neither is Infinity.

A whole number beyond 2^53 - 1 would be changed by a binary64 reader (9007199254740993 becomes 9007199254740992), so the call is refused before anything can change it; such a number is sent as a string.
The same, for a number of twenty digits.
A number with an exponent that no binary64 holds.
Half of a surrogate pair on its own is not text.
The same, in a key.
An input that is not JSON is refused, never shown as if it were.
So is no input at all.
A tool's input is an object.
A number with a leading zero is not JSON.
Nesting stops at 64.
A call names its tool.
A request for a tool call: its digest is the SHA-256 of the UTF-8 bytes of effect_text, which is the whole effect as RFC 8785 writes it, and its lines are the lines of that effect.
Accented text in the input and in the directory, and a fraction written 1.50 by the engine: the bound text holds the text itself and the number as 1.5, and the lines show the same.
A plugin effect, under csl-cj/v0 as before: every field of it, and every field of its payload, is on a line.

A file name with a right-to-left override in it (it would read notes/exe.png on a terminal), a zero-width space and U+007F. The bound text holds them as they are; the lines show each as an escape, so what is drawn cannot be reordered or hidden.

The effect is a Write to a menu file; the lines are those of a Bash call that removes a build folder. The owner would be shown one thing and approve another. (This is the mistake the first draft's fixtures made.)
The digest is the SHA-256 of no bytes at all, not of the effect.
The digest is another effect's: an answer that names it would approve that other effect.
The digest is taken over the same effect as an everyday serialiser writes it, with escapes for the accented letters. Those are other bytes, so it is another digest: one canonical form, one digest.
The last field of the input is not on a line. Nothing may be hidden.
A line nobody bound is added, in the core's own voice.
The engine's own text is marked as the core's.
A plugin effect drawn as one line of summary: the payload's fields (what is bought, how much) are not shown.
The lines carry the right-to-left override raw instead of as an escape: on a terminal the file name would read as another.
The call holds a whole number beyond 2^53 - 1. A schema cannot refuse it; the profile does, so the record has no canonical bytes, no digest and no lines.
An opening that names revision 2 on a request that is at revision 1.
The same principal on the same surface at the same revision is recorded once.

One request from the moment the core drew it: an answer before any showing, two surfaces showing it, a wrong digest, a stale revision, the answer, the same command again, the same command id with another answer, a second answer, an engine trying to answer, and a look after it is settled.
A plugin effect: shown on the command line, then approved there.

Seven events of one log and the seven lines of its transcript: each line's seq, time, type, source, trust and state are its event's, and so is its text where the text is the event's own. The sentences, what is announced and where input goes are the renderer's.

The third event carries an earlier time than the second: the clock stepped back. Its line keeps the time of the line before, so the transcript never runs backwards; the fourth goes on from the real clock.
The second line says 1,840 ms; its event is 2,074 ms after the first. (The first draft's fixtures had this mistake.)

The engine's output is a whole line of its stream; the transcript line shows a sentence taken out of it. The text of an engine.output line is the payload's text, not a reading of it. (The first draft's fixtures had this mistake too.)
The turn ended 'waiting'; its line says 'done'.
A line of engine output marked as coming from the core and trusted.
One line for each event, in order: here the last event has none.
An event dated the 31st of February. The timestamp pattern lets it through; the rule refuses it, so no transcript is made from a log that holds it.
After the clock stepped back, the line shows the smaller time instead of keeping the one before.

A message waiting for the next turn. Its intent to deliver is committed first; then it is written toward the engine, which changes nothing in the record; it is 'delivered' only when the engine's own acceptance names its delivery id, and then it carries the turn it began.
The daemon stops after it committed the intent and BEFORE it wrote anything. At the restart the item is outcome_unknown: shown as sent and not confirmed, and never sent again by itself.

The daemon stops AFTER the write returned and before any acceptance arrived. The record is the same as when it stops before the write, and so is the end: outcome_unknown. One commit cannot make a delivery to an engine happen exactly once; what it can do is never claim a delivery nobody confirmed and never send twice.
A steer message is written into the turn in progress. steer.sent records the write and changes nothing in the item; the engine's acceptance, how mid_turn, makes it delivered into that same turn.

A steer message was written into a turn, and the turn ended with no acceptance of it from the engine: nobody can say whether the engine read it. It is outcome_unknown, not delivered and not queued again.
An edit while the item is queued raises its revision. Once the intent to deliver is committed, it can be neither edited nor withdrawn.
An item withdrawn while it was queued cannot begin delivery.
Only an acceptance that names THIS delivery makes the item delivered. One that names another, or one that arrives for an item nothing was committed for, changes nothing.
A restart, and the end of a turn, change only an item that was being delivered. A queued item stays queued and is delivered later, once.
A turn in progress. The Task is created when the first event of the turn was logged, and last changed at its latest state.changed: the times the core logged.
An approval is pending for the turn: a person must answer it on a surface that draws approvals. It is never answered through the Task.
The turn ended and its work is done. The result is the turn's own, and it expires when the turn's does.
The turn is over, so the Task is completed; its outcome says the engine waits for the user, which is not 'done'.
The turn failed with a typed code. The worker is gone.
Cancelling a turn's Task is an interrupt of that turn, not a Stop: the Task is cancelled because the turn's outcome is 'interrupted', and the worker lives on.
The run was stopped and the Stop was confirmed: the turn's Task is cancelled. 'cancelled' is never shown before that.
A Stop of the session was asked and is not confirmed: the turn is still working, with cancel_requested true.
A turn that waits behind the turn in progress: it is bound to no run yet, and its only event is the one that recorded it.
An earlier turn of a run that a later turn shares. Its Task carries its own result and its own times; nothing of the later turn, though that one ended last on the same run.
Work started with run.start and no session: the Task id is the run id, there is no session and no turn, and it does not expire. Its times are those of the run's own log, 'run:<run_id>'.
A run that is being started: working. Its log holds one event so far, so both times are that event's.
An approval is pending for the run.
A Stop was asked and is not confirmed. The Task keeps the status it had, working, and says cancel_requested. It is not 'cancelled'.
The Stop is confirmed: only now is the Task cancelled.
The run ended and its result says ok: completed. The Task carries the result's code and detail and names the run as where the whole result is read (run.status).
The run ended and its result is an error: failed, with the result's own code.
A result that breaks the route contract's own rule: it says ok and carries a code. The Task goes by the code: failed, never completed.
The other way to break it: the result says error and names no code. The Task is failed, with the code result_invalid, and invents no reason.
The run ended and there is no result to read: failed, with the code result_unavailable. It is never shown as completed.

A start that never launched, as the record is today: nothing durable says why, so the code is start_failed and the detail is null. The log holds nothing of it either, so both times are null. The Task invents none of this.
RESERVED: the same, once the record carries start_error (the lane that owns Stop writes it). The Task's detail is then that code.
The machine restarted under the run: failed, with the code lost_reboot.
The unit cannot be observed: nobody can say that the run ended, so the Task is still working.
A Stop is pending and the Task already says cancelled. 'cancelled' is shown only once the Stop is confirmed.
The record of a start that never launched keeps no reason, and the Task gives one. After a restart nothing could back it.
The record carries start_error and the Task's detail is null.
The run ended with no result kept, and the Task says completed.
The Task of an earlier turn carries the result of the turn that ended last on the same run.
Both times are the moment the Task was asked for, not the times the core logged.
Nothing is stopping the session, and the Task of its turn says cancel_requested.
An approval is pending for the run and the Task says working, with no approval named.
